::: {.why}
The same picture as week 15, in a different problem, and the useful part is that here the risk being traded against is over minutes rather than years, which makes the preference easier to state.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Draw the execution efficient frontier for a specific order and identify the schedule at a stated risk aversion.
- Say how the frontier's shape changes with the order's size relative to daily volume.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Trace the frontier: expected implementation cost against its standard deviation, across the family of optimal schedules, for a specific order size in a specific name using your fitted impact model. Mark TWAP on it and note that it sits at one end rather than in the middle.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Vary the size: redraw the frontier for orders at 0.5, 2 and 10 percent of daily volume. The frontier moves out and its shape changes, and with your fitted square-root exponent the cost scales sublinearly, which is a different picture from the linear-impact version in the original paper.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Implement the schedule generator in qlib/exec/schedule.py, taking an order, a horizon and a risk aversion, and returning a target trajectory.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
qlib/exec/schedule.py generates an execution trajectory from an order, a horizon and a stated risk aversion, using the fitted impact model rather than the linear assumption in the original paper.
:::

## Resources

- [Almgren & Chriss (2000) — Optimal Execution of Portfolio Transactions](https://www.smallake.kr/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/optliq.pdf) [paper]{.res-kind}
- [Tóth et al. (2011) — Anomalous price impact and the critical nature of liquidity](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.1694) [paper]{.res-kind}
